chunks: Ali ibn Ja'far narrated from his brother Musa (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a mukatab (a slave who has agreed to pay a specific sum for his freedom), whether the fitrah of the month of Ramadan is upon him or upon the one who contracted with him, and whether his testimony is valid. He said: 'The fitrah is upon him, and his testimony is not valid.'

key_terms.تَجُوزُ: Is valid/permissible, indicating the acceptance of a legal act or testimony.
key_terms.شَهَادَتُهُ: His testimony, referring to the legal validity of a person's witness account in Islamic courts.
key_terms.فِطْرَةُ: Fitrah, the alms paid by each Muslim at the end of Ramadan to purify the fasting person.
key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has entered into a contract with his master to pay a specific sum for his manumission.

ai.seo_question: Is a mukatab responsible for paying fitrah and is his testimony valid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that a mukatab remains personally liable for the fitrah of Ramadan, distinguishing this obligation from that of the master who freed him. Furthermore, the Imam affirms the validity of the mukatab's testimony in legal matters, reflecting his transitional status as a free person in terms of judicial capacity despite not yet being fully emancipated. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that the mukatab's financial and legal responsibilities are distinct from those of a slave, aligning with the broader principles of justice in Islamic law.
